note: Typical mistakes are tendencies, not rules about people. They happen because your first language has different sounds, letters or rules: this is called transfer (or interference). Not everyone makes these mistakes, and many learners stop making them quite quickly. If you know where a mistake comes from, you get rid of it faster. Based on comparing the language systems (contrastive linguistics) and on experience from language teaching.

languages.name: English
strengths: English and Portuguese share thousands of words from Latin: hospital, animal, importante, família, universidade.
Many English words ending in -tion, -ty or -ent have a Portuguese twin: informação, cidade, importante. Learn the endings -ção, -dade and -mente and you gain hundreds of words.
Word order in simple sentences (subject, verb, object) is the same as in English.

mistakes.wrong: bom as “bone”, bem as “bem” with a clear m
mistakes.right: bom, bem: nasal vowel, no clear m
mistakes.why: English has no nasal vowels, only nasal consonants. Let air go through your nose and don't close the sound with m or n.
English speakers hear a final n or an English diphthong. The Portuguese ending is a nasal vowel gliding on to a short w or y.

mistakes.wrong: carro, rato with an English r (tongue curled back)
mistakes.right: carro, rato: strong r at the back · caro: one tap
mistakes.why: English r doesn't touch anything. Portuguese has two r sounds, a quick tap and a strong back r, and they make different words.

mistakes.wrong: avó, avô both with English “oh” (a glide)
mistakes.right: avó: open o · avô: closed o, no glide
mistakes.why: English stressed vowels glide (“go”, “day”). Portuguese vowels stay still, and open or closed can change the word.

mistakes.wrong: chá, chave with ch as in “church”
mistakes.why: English ch is t + sh. Portuguese ch is just sh.

mistakes.wrong: já, gente with the j of “jam”
mistakes.why: English j starts with a stop (d + zh). In Portuguese j and g before e, i have no stop.

mistakes.wrong: hoje, hotel with a breathy h
mistakes.why: English h is said. Portuguese h is always silent.
English has no single lh sound. Say it with the middle of the tongue against the roof of your mouth.
In English you ‘are’ 25. In Portuguese you ‘have’ years: tenho 25 anos. The same goes for fome, sede, frio and calor.
Gostar always takes de. English ‘like’ takes no preposition, so the de is easy to forget. The subject pronoun eu is usually left out.
Portuguese has two verbs for ‘to be’. Ser is for what someone or something is (identity, origin, profession); estar is for how someone is now (tired, in Lisbon, ill).
Most city names take no article: a Lisboa, em Lisboa, de Lisboa. A few do (o Porto, o Funchal): vou ao Porto. Learn these as exceptions.
Most adjectives go after the noun. A few common ones (bom, mau, grande, novo) can go before it, but the safe default is after.
Adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number: a casa bonita, os livros caros. English adjectives never change.

mistakes.right: Espero pelo autocarro. / Estou à espera do autocarro.
mistakes.why: English ‘wait for’ becomes esperar por or estar à espera de. Esperar para would mean ‘to wait in order to’.

mistakes.wrong: Atualmente, não gosto de café. (meaning: actually, I don’t like coffee)
mistakes.right: Na verdade, não gosto de café.
mistakes.why: Atualmente means ‘at the moment’, not ‘actually’. It is a classic false friend: use na verdade or de facto for ‘actually’.
Portuguese writes languages, days and months with a small letter (inglês, segunda-feira, janeiro).

languages.name: German
strengths: Portuguese verbs change for the person, as German ones do: eu vou, tu vais, ele vai.
You already know the difference between du and Sie. Portuguese has tu, você and o senhor / a senhora, which work in a similar way (o senhor is closest to Sie).
Nouns have a gender, as in German, and Portuguese has only two.

mistakes.wrong: pequeno, telefone with a full e (“pe-KE-no”)
mistakes.why: German reduces e only at the end of a word (Gabe, bitte). In Portuguese unstressed e in the middle and at the start nearly vanishes too.
German has no nasal vowels except in French loan words (Pension). Let air go through your nose and add a short w or y.

mistakes.wrong: bom as “bohm”, um as “um” with a clear m
mistakes.right: bom: nasal vowel, no clear m
mistakes.why: German vowels before m or n are not nasal. In Portuguese the vowel is nasal and the m or n is hardly heard.

mistakes.wrong: mas, festa, luz with a clear s
mistakes.why: In German, sch only appears for s in st and sp at the start (Stein). In Portuguese every s before a consonant or at the end of a word is sh or zh.
German j is y. Portuguese j and g before e, i are the sound of French j (je).

mistakes.wrong: chá with the German ach- or ich-sound
mistakes.why: German ch is a back or front fricative. Portuguese ch is sh, as German sch.

mistakes.wrong: hoje, hotel with a breathy h
mistakes.why: German h is said. Portuguese h is silent.

mistakes.wrong: os amigos with a small stop before “amigos”
mistakes.why: German starts a word that begins with a vowel with a small throat stop. Portuguese links the words, and a final s even becomes z.

mistakes.wrong: falar, mulher with a vowel-like r (“falaa”)
mistakes.right: falar: a weak tap at the end
mistakes.why: German final -r is a vowel (Vater). Portuguese final r is a quick tap or very weak r, not a vowel.

mistakes.wrong: A minha filha vai ao ginásio. (meaning: she goes to a Gymnasium)
mistakes.right: A minha filha vai à escola secundária.
mistakes.why: O ginásio is a gym. The school you know as Gymnasium is the escola secundária in Portugal (people also say liceu, an older word).
A taxa is a fee or a rate (a taxa de juro, taxas moderadoras). A cup is a chávena in Portugal (Brazilians say xícara).
In German you ‘are’ 30 years old, in Portuguese you have them: tenho 30 anos.

mistakes.wrong: Eu sou em casa. Eu sou cansado.
mistakes.why: Place and state take estar, not ser. Where German has just ‘sein’, Portuguese asks: is it lasting (ser) or a place or state (estar)?

mistakes.wrong: Ontem tenho trabalhado até às seis.
mistakes.why: German uses the Perfekt for the past (ich habe gearbeitet). In Portuguese, a finished event uses the pretérito perfeito simples: trabalhei. Tenho trabalhado means something else (a repeated action up to now).
The genders are the opposite of German (die Sonne, der Mond). Learn the article together with the word.

mistakes.wrong: No Verão falo Português com os meus Amigos.
mistakes.right: No verão falo português com os meus amigos.
mistakes.why: German capitalises every noun. In Portuguese only names and the first word of a sentence start with a capital.

languages.name: French
strengths: French and Portuguese come from Latin and share a lot of grammar: gender, articles, the past tenses and the subjunctive.
Many words are close: famille – família, université – universidade, liberté – liberdade.
You already know that the verb ending shows the person, and you know the idea of a formal and an informal ‘you’.

mistakes.wrong: bom as French “bon”, bem as French “bain”
mistakes.why: French has nasal vowels too, but the Portuguese ones are different: more closed, and often with a glide at the end.

mistakes.wrong: avó, avô and pode, pôde mixed up
mistakes.right: follow the accent: é, ó open · ê, ô closed
mistakes.why: French has open and closed e and o too, but the pairs do not always match the Portuguese ones. Follow the written accent.

mistakes.wrong: stress on the last syllable of every word
mistakes.right: telefone: stress on fo · está, falámos
mistakes.why: French stress falls on the last syllable of the phrase. Every Portuguese word has its own strong syllable, and the accent can change the word (falámos, falamos).

mistakes.wrong: os amigos, mas with a silent final s
mistakes.why: In French a final s is silent. In Portuguese it is said: sh before a consonant or at the end, z before a vowel.
French ill is just y. Portuguese lh is a palatal l: the tongue touches the roof of your mouth. nh is the same as French gn.
Don't add a clear n or split the diphthong. Start with the nasal vowel and glide to a short w.

mistakes.wrong: azul, papel with a clear French l
mistakes.why: A French l is always clear. In Portugal l at the end of a syllable is dark.
French quitter becomes deixar in Portuguese. Quitar does not mean ‘to leave’.
French attendre = esperar. Atender means to answer (the phone) or to serve (a customer): atender o telefone.
Portuguese has no partitive article (du, de la). You say quero pão, bebo água, comprei leite.

mistakes.wrong: Eu falo português e eu vivo em Lisboa.
mistakes.right: Falo português e vivo em Lisboa.
mistakes.why: French needs the subject pronoun every time. Portuguese leaves it out: the verb ending already says who. Use eu or tu only for contrast.
French depuis for a length of time becomes há (há duas semanas). Desde is for a starting point: desde segunda-feira.
Some genders differ from French (le pont, l’arbre are masculine, but a ponte, a árvore are feminine). Learn the article with the noun.
Portuguese spells the f-sound with f, not ph: farmácia, telefone, filosofia, fotografia.

languages.name: Spanish
strengths: Portuguese and Spanish share most of their vocabulary and grammar: casa, ter – tener, falar – hablar, muito – mucho.
You can read Portuguese almost at once, and you will understand a lot of it at the first listen.
Ser and estar work in much the same way in both languages.
The big risk is the opposite: because it feels easy, you stop listening and mix the two languages (people call it portuñol). Treat Portuguese as its own language from day one.

mistakes.why: Spanish vowels keep their full sound in every syllable. In Portugal unstressed vowels, above all e, are weak or lost. You will be understood, but you will sound foreign, and fast speech will be hard to follow.

mistakes.wrong: livro, banco with a clear Spanish o
mistakes.why: A Spanish final -o is a clear o. In Portugal an unstressed final o sounds like u.

mistakes.wrong: avó, avô both with the same Spanish o
mistakes.why: Spanish has one e and one o. Portuguese has open and closed ones, and the accent shows which; it can change the word (pode, pôde).

mistakes.wrong: bom, bem with a clear m (“bom-m”)
mistakes.right: bom, bem: nasal vowel, hardly any m
mistakes.why: In Spanish a vowel + n or m has a full consonant. In Portuguese the vowel is nasal and the consonant almost disappears.
Spanish has no nasal diphthongs. Say each of them as one syllable, with air through the nose.

mistakes.wrong: mas, festa, português with a Spanish s
mistakes.why: Spanish s stays s (or fades in the south). In Portugal s before a consonant or at the end of a word is sh or zh.

mistakes.wrong: casa as “kasa” with a sharp s
mistakes.why: A Spanish s never buzzes before a vowel. In Portuguese a single s between vowels is z, and casa and caça are different words.

mistakes.wrong: falar, mulher with a strong trill at the end of the word
mistakes.right: falar: a very weak final r
mistakes.why: A Spanish final r is a clear tap. In Portuguese it is weak, and the strong r is usually made at the back of the mouth (a trill is understood, but sounds northern or old-fashioned).
Spanish ll is now y for most speakers. Portuguese lh is a real palatal l. nh is the same sound as Spanish ñ.

mistakes.wrong: já, gente with a Spanish j (a rasp)
mistakes.why: Spanish j is a rasp at the back of the mouth. Portuguese j is a soft, buzzing sh.

mistakes.wrong: chá, chave as the Spanish ch (“church”)
mistakes.why: Spanish ch is t + sh. Portuguese ch is just sh. Careful: the two sounds are swapped between the languages.

mistakes.wrong: azul, papel with a clear Spanish l
mistakes.why: A Spanish l is always clear. In Portugal l at the end of a syllable is dark.
Muy does not exist in Portuguese: it is muito, for ‘very’ and ‘much’ alike. Obrigado (said by a man) / obrigada (said by a woman) replaces gracias.
Tengo becomes tenho (nh, not ng). Spanish forms leak into Portuguese, especially irregular verbs: tengo/tenho, hago/faço, pongo/ponho.
Gostar de is a regular verb in Portuguese: gosto, gostas, gosta. It does not work like gustar (me gusta). Portuguese also leaves out the article here: gosto de café.
Hay becomes há (with an accent). Há also means ‘ago’ or ‘for’ in time expressions: há dois anos.
No accent on tu in Portuguese, and the verb is és, not eres or es: tu és, ele é.
Spanish voy a + infinitive. Portuguese uses vou + infinitive without a: vou comprar, vou sair. Estar a + infinitive does take a: estou a comprar.

mistakes.right: Estou a falar com o senhorio.
mistakes.why: In Portugal the standard way to say ‘I am doing’ is estar a + infinitive: estou a falar. Estou falando (gerund, like Spanish estoy hablando) is the Brazilian way. You will hear it, but do not use it as your default in Portugal.

mistakes.wrong: Vivo en el Porto. Vou a Lisboa en comboio.
mistakes.right: Vivo no Porto. Vou a Lisboa de comboio.
mistakes.why: Em + o = no, em + a = na: Portuguese contracts the preposition with the article. For a vehicle you say de comboio, de autocarro (or num comboio).
Esquisito means odd or strange, not ‘exquisite’. For tasty say delicioso or saboroso.

mistakes.wrong: Estou embaraçada de cinco meses. (meaning: pregnant)
mistakes.why: Embaraçado means embarrassed, awkward. Pregnant is grávida (not embarazada).
The Spanish ñ is nh in Portuguese (senhor, amanhã), and ll is lh or ch (filho, chamo-me). There is no ñ in Portuguese.

languages.name: Italian
strengths: Italian and Portuguese share a lot of vocabulary: casa, amico – amigo, libro – livro.
Like Portuguese, Italian usually leaves out the subject: parlo – falo.
You already know the contraction of preposition and article (nel, sul, dal), so no (em + o) and do (de + o) are not a surprise.

mistakes.why: Italian vowels keep their full sound in every syllable. In Portugal unstressed vowels, above all e, are weak or lost.

mistakes.wrong: livro, banco with a clear Italian o
mistakes.why: An Italian final -o is a clear o. In Portugal an unstressed final o sounds like u.

mistakes.wrong: pessoa with a long “ss”, carro with a long “rr”
mistakes.why: Italian has long double consonants. In Portuguese rr and ss are one short sound each.

mistakes.wrong: mas, festa with a clear s
mistakes.why: Italian s stays s before consonants (festa, sport). In Portugal s before a consonant or at the end of a word is sh or zh.
In Italian, s between vowels varies by region. In Portuguese it is always z, and ss, ç are the sharp s (casa, caça).

mistakes.wrong: bom, um as Italian “bon”, “un” with a clear n or m
mistakes.right: nasal vowel, no clear n or m
mistakes.why: Italian has no nasal vowels. Let air go through your nose and don't close the sound.
Say each as one syllable: a nasal vowel gliding to a short w or y.

mistakes.wrong: azul, Portugal with a clear Italian l
mistakes.why: An Italian l is always clear. In Portugal l at the end of a syllable is dark.
Burro in Portuguese means donkey, and also ‘stupid’. Butter is manteiga.
Caldo is broth (caldo verde). Hot weather is calor: está calor, está quente.
Italian uses essere with verbs of movement (sono andato). Portuguese uses the simple past (fui) or ter + participle only for repeated actions.
Italian essere covers ser and estar. In Portuguese, temporary states and places take estar.
em + o = no, em + a = na, de + o = do, a + o = ao. In Portuguese this contraction is always written.
Plural: add -s (casas, livros). The Italian plural -i/-e does not exist in Portuguese.
Portuguese has hardly any double consonants (except rr and ss between vowels): diferente, possível. -ibile becomes -ível and -agine becomes -agem.

languages.name: Romanian
strengths: Romanian is a Romance language too, and many words are close: casă – casa, carne – carne, apă – água.
The verb ending shows the person, so you can leave out the subject, as in Portuguese: vorbesc – falo.

mistakes.why: Romanian carte = book. In Portuguese, carta is a letter (or a playing card). A book is livro.
Romanian puts the article at the end of the noun (omul). Portuguese puts it before: o homem, a casa.
Romanian uses one verb (a fi) for both. In Portuguese, states and places take estar.
Romanian vreau să merg uses the subjunctive. When the subject stays the same, Portuguese uses the infinitive: quero ir.

languages.name: Arabic
strengths: Portuguese has hundreds of words from Arabic: azeite, açúcar, almofada, alface, armazém, aldeia, oxalá.
Nouns have a gender, and the adjective usually comes after the noun: casa branca.
The verb form shows the person, so you can often leave out the subject.

mistakes.wrong: olá, chamo-me ana e vivo em lisboa.
mistakes.right: Olá, chamo-me Ana e vivo em Lisboa.
mistakes.why: Arabic has no capital letters. In Portuguese, names and the first word of a sentence start with a capital (days, months and languages do not).
Arabic has no ‘is’ in the present. Portuguese needs ser or estar in every sentence: é médico, está em Lisboa.
In Arabic a relative clause repeats a pronoun for the object. Portuguese does not: o livro que comprei.
The genders are the opposite of Arabic: o sol is masculine, a lua is feminine.

languages.name: Russian
strengths: Nouns have a gender and verbs change for the person, so neither idea is new to you.
Like Portuguese, Russian uses a double negative: я ничего не знаю – não sei nada.

mistakes.why: Russian has no articles. In Portuguese nouns almost always carry one: o, a, os, as, um, uma.
Russian drops ‘to be’ in the present. In Portuguese the verb is always there: sou, és, é, estou.
Russian мне 30 лет has no verb. Portuguese says tenho 30 anos.
The adjective usually follows the noun in Portuguese.

languages.name: Ukrainian
strengths: Nouns have a gender and verbs change for the person, so neither idea is new to you.
A yes/no question can be made with the voice alone, as in Portuguese: Ти хочеш чаю? – Queres chá?

mistakes.why: Ukrainian has no articles. In Portuguese a noun nearly always has one.
Ukrainian drops ‘to be’ in the present. Portuguese always says it: sou professora.
Gostar takes de: gosto de café, gosto de ti.
Ligar a alguém is the common pattern in Portugal (ligo à minha mãe; ligo-lhe). Also note the article before the possessive: a minha mãe.

languages.name: Chinese
strengths: Like Portuguese, Chinese puts the subject first, then the verb, then the object: 我喝咖啡 – bebo café.
Chinese often leaves out ‘I’ when it is clear, and Portuguese does that all the time.

mistakes.why: The verb changes for the person: trabalho, trabalhas, trabalha… Do not use the infinitive as the main verb.
Portuguese marks the plural with -s on the noun, and adjectives agree in gender and number.
Chinese shows time with a word like ‘yesterday’. Portuguese changes the verb as well: fui (past), vou (now or soon).
Chinese has no articles. Portuguese nouns normally have one.

quiz.prompt: Why do many learners with Arabic as their first language write names with a small letter?
options: Their script has no capital letters
In Arabic everything is written in capitals
quiz.answer: Their script has no capital letters
quiz.explain: In Portuguese, names and the first word of a sentence start with a capital letter.

quiz.prompt: How do you say your age correctly?
quiz.explain: Sou 25 anos comes from English or German. Portuguese uses ter.
For ‘actually’ say na verdade or de facto. Atualmente is a false friend for English speakers.

quiz.prompt: You moved here three years ago and you still live here. What is correct?
options: Vivo aqui por três anos há.
quiz.explain: Há + a length of time. Desde goes with a starting point: desde 2023.

quiz.prompt: You like books. What do you say?
Where does the adjective usually go in Portuguese?
options: After the noun: uma casa branca
Before the noun: uma branca casa
quiz.answer: After the noun: uma casa branca
quiz.explain: A few short adjectives (bom, mau, grande) can go before, but after is the safe default.

quiz.prompt: How do you say ‘I am speaking’ in standard Portugal Portuguese?
quiz.explain: Estar a + infinitive is the European form. Estou falando is the Brazilian one.

quiz.prompt: You feel cold. What do you say?
quiz.explain: How your body feels goes with ter: tenho frio, calor, fome, sede, sono.

quiz.prompt: What is o ginásio in Portugal?
quiz.explain: A secondary school is a escola secundária. Ginásio is a false friend for German speakers.
